text: In 1857, the Company gave its Indian soldiers a new rifle.
To load it, you had to bite open a paper cartridge.
A rumor spread like fire.
The cartridges were greased with cow and pig fat, offensive to Hindus and Muslims alike.
At Meerut, soldiers who refused them were jailed.
Their comrades rose up, freed them, and marched to Delhi, where they declared the old Mughal
Emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, ruler of India again.
The revolt spread across the north, and one of its fiercest leaders was a young widow
the company had tried to retire, Anani Lakshmibai of Jhansi.
When her husband died, the company refused to accept her adopted son as heir and simply
took her kingdom.
She was handed a pension and told to step aside.
In 1857, she stepped back in. She led her troops on horseback and died fighting. In
her late twenties, she became the most famous face of the revolt. The British crushed the
rising with terrible brutality. Pole villages were burned. Bahadur Shah's offer was exiled
to Burma. The Mughal dynasty, after 330 years, was over. London decided the company could
not be trusted with India anymore. In 1858 the British crown took over directly. The
Raj had begun. Your Majesty, India is now ruled by the crown. Splendid. And the company?
Closed. Your Majesty. Then I shall need a new title. Empress of India, ma'am? Now that's
a title. She got it. In 1876, India gave Britain smaller things too. In 1814, an Indian businessman
opened a bathhouse in Brighton, offering a head massage called Champa. Today, you'd call it
shampoo. Under the Raj, India got railways. Remember those bricks from Harappa? Same railway
age. The tracks ran mainly to carry raw cotton to the ports and British factory cloth back in.
about that. India, the land of Calico and Chintz, the land that once dressed half the
world, now bought its cloth from Manchester. And the famines kept coming. In the great
famine of 1876, millions died while grain was still being exported.
Then an Indian thinker named Dadabai Naoroji sat down with the numbers. Remember Pliny,
the Roman who complained that India drained Rome of its gold,
Narrowji made the same complaint the other way around.
He called it the drain of wealth,
India's money flowing out to Britain year after year.
But the British also built schools, newspapers, and universities.
And in them, a new generation of Indians
learned exactly how to argue with an empire.
One of them was a young lawyer about to be thrown off a train.
